<reason>A narrow win for PRO. The decisive clash was demand elasticity: A attacked it with budget-capped, satiated organizational demand and cost-center margin logic, while B countered with the revenue-share/competitive-forcing loop. Both mechanisms were asserted rather than proven, leaving rough parity on the first clause, but A framed the choice more decisively ("does a cheaper cost center hire more or fewer people?") and kept the observable hiring-freeze evidence on the table. B landed two genuinely strong hits—the motion-shift charge on transition friction and the "tautology" critique of A counting only centrally-created AI jobs—but never neutralized A's asymmetric-risk argument for the policy clause, and B's own concession that "portable benefits can be argued on their own" weakened its preparation-harms case. B's clipped opening and slightly less memorable framing cost it at the margins. Both sides answered pressure questions directly and crystallized cleanly; A simply made the debate marginally easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's B4.5 charge that A's "AI itself creates" framing is a tautology—defining creation as a thin central staff so destruction wins by construction—was the sharpest single hit of the debate, forcing A onto the defensive about burden-shifting. A's best answer was the cost-center satiation mechanism in A2.2-A2.3, which met B's strongest card (demand expansion) head-on and set up the closing's one-question framing; that sustained, direct engagement across multiple rounds gave A the edge in the exchange overall.</best_rebuttal>
